parts.move: state the mean kinetic-energy temperature relation
parts.prompt: State the kinetic-theory relation linking mean molecular kinetic energy to absolute temperature.
scheme: ½m⟨c²⟩ = 3/2 kT
T is absolute temperature in kelvin and ⟨c²⟩ is the mean square molecular speed
parts.answer: The relation is ½m⟨c²⟩ = 3/2 kT, with T in kelvin and ⟨c²⟩ the mean square molecular speed.

parts.move: identify absolute temperature as the scale required by kinetic theory
parts.prompt: Why must temperature be expressed in kelvin in the kinetic-theory equation?
scheme: The equation relates kinetic energy to absolute temperature measured from the zero-energy limit
A Celsius reading must be converted using T/K = θ/°C + 273.15
parts.answer: Kinetic theory uses absolute temperature, measured from the zero-energy limit. Convert Celsius by adding 273.15 to obtain kelvin.

parts.move: explain pressure increase from greater molecular momentum transfer
parts.prompt: A sealed rigid container is heated. Explain, using molecular collisions, why its pressure rises.
scheme: Heating raises the mean molecular kinetic energy and speed
Faster molecules change momentum more rapidly and transfer more momentum to the fixed walls per second, increasing force per area
parts.answer: Heating increases molecular speeds. Collisions then change momentum more often and by larger amounts, so the force on the fixed walls per area, the pressure, increases.

parts.move: explain temperature as an average over random molecular motion
parts.prompt: Two samples of the same gas have equal temperature but different numbers of molecules. Explain what is equal and what is not.
scheme: Equal temperature means equal mean translational kinetic energy per molecule
The larger sample has more total internal kinetic energy because it contains more molecules
parts.answer: Temperature fixes the mean kinetic energy per molecule. A sample with more molecules has the same average but a larger total molecular kinetic energy.

parts.move: predict a pressure change from temperature and fixed volume
parts.prompt: A gas in a rigid vessel is warmed from 300 K to 450 K. If its initial pressure is 1.20 × 10⁵ Pa, calculate the new pressure.
scheme: At fixed volume p/T is constant
parts.answer: Since p/T is constant, p₂ = 1.20×10⁵(450/300) = 1.80×10⁵ Pa.

parts.move: use the kinetic-energy relation to find a molecular speed
parts.prompt: Estimate the root-mean-square speed of helium atoms at 300 K. Take helium atom mass as 6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg and k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.
scheme: ½m⟨c²⟩ = 3/2 kT, so crms = √(3kT/m)
crms = 1.37 × 10³ m s⁻¹

parts.move: reject equality of every molecular speed at one temperature
parts.prompt: A student says all molecules in a gas at 300 K move at exactly the same speed. Correct the statement.
scheme: Temperature specifies a mean (or mean-square) kinetic energy, not one speed for every molecule
Molecules have a distribution of speeds and collide continually
parts.answer: At 300 K the mean-square kinetic energy is fixed, but individual molecules have a range of speeds. Temperature does not make every molecule move at one identical speed.

parts.move: distinguish Celsius zero from the zero-energy limit
parts.prompt: Why is 0 °C not the temperature at which molecular motion stops?
scheme: 0 °C corresponds to 273.15 K, not 0 K
The kinetic-theory zero-energy limit is absolute zero at 0 K (an unattainable ideal limit)
parts.answer: 0 °C is 273.15 K. Molecular kinetic energy would approach its minimum only as absolute temperature approaches 0 K, not at the Celsius ice point.

parts.move: compare mean translational energies per particle for two gases at one temperature
parts.prompt: At 350 K, compare the mean translational kinetic energy per neon atom with that per helium atom. Calculate each value and state the ratio. Take k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.
scheme: For either ideal gas the mean translational energy per particle is 3/2 kT = 7.25 × 10⁻²¹ J
The values are equal, so the neon-to-helium ratio is 1:1; molecular mass changes speed distribution, not mean energy at fixed T
parts.answer: For both gases Ē = 3/2 kT = 1.5(1.38×10⁻²³)(350) = 7.25×10⁻²¹ J per atom. The ratio is 1:1; at fixed temperature mass changes the speed distribution, not the mean energy per particle.

parts.move: invert the kinetic-theory relation to find absolute temperature
parts.prompt: Argon atoms of mass 6.63 × 10⁻²⁶ kg have an rms speed of 420 m s⁻¹. Estimate their temperature using k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.
scheme: Use ½mcrms² = 3/2 kT, so T = mcrms²/(3k)

parts.move: transfer the temperature-energy relation to a different planetary atmosphere
parts.prompt: At the same temperature, nitrogen molecules on Mars and Earth have the same mean translational kinetic energy. What differs if the atmospheric pressure is lower on Mars?
scheme: Same T gives the same mean kinetic energy per molecule for the same molecular species
Lower pressure can result from fewer molecules per unit volume and/or different volume density, not lower energy per molecule
parts.answer: For the same nitrogen species and T, 3/2 kT is the same per molecule. Mars can have lower pressure because it has fewer molecules per unit volume, not because each molecule has less mean energy.

parts.move: connect random molecular energy with a temperature-dependent material property
parts.prompt: Why can the speed of sound in a gas change when the gas is heated, even at the same pressure?
scheme: Heating changes the mean molecular speed and therefore how rapidly pressure disturbances are transmitted
The detailed speed also depends on the gas compressibility and density; temperature is not simply a change in wave frequency
parts.answer: Heating raises molecular speeds, so pressure disturbances are transmitted faster. The exact sound speed also depends on the gas density and compressibility.

parts.move: link molecular pressure work to macroscopic engine power
parts.prompt: In a piston engine, hot gas expands and pushes the piston. Explain how the kinetic-theory picture accounts for positive work during this stroke.
scheme: Heating gives molecules greater mean kinetic energy and more energetic wall collisions
The gas pressure acts over the piston displacement, doing positive work on the piston
The gas's internal energy decreases if the work output exceeds heat supplied during the stroke
parts.answer: Hotter molecules collide with the piston more energetically, producing pressure. Pressure acting through the piston displacement does positive work; if that work exceeds heat input, the gas internal energy falls.

parts.move: combine a temperature measurement uncertainty with a kinetic-energy conclusion
parts.prompt: A gas thermometer reads 300 ± 6 K. What percentage uncertainty should be assigned to the mean molecular kinetic energy inferred from 3/2 kT?
scheme: Mean kinetic energy is directly proportional to T
Percentage uncertainty = 6/300 × 100 = 2%
parts.answer: Because Ēk = 3/2 kT is proportional to T, the percentage uncertainty is (6/300)×100 = 2%.
